title: Pre-decode EX control in ID: one-hot ALU result select, early forwarding match, piped PC+4
motivation:
All three baseline P&R seeds (128.72 / 127.03 / 123.02 MHz) share one critical
path. It starts at the ID/EX alu_op bits (id_ex_w[50..54]) and passes through
about 12 LUT4/MUX2_LUT5 levels into the EX/MEM alu_result flops. Those levels
are the 5-bit alu_op decode, which ABC merges into the 19-way result case
(shifter, logic ops, SLT, divider special-case muxes and the multiplier-sharing
operand muxes yosys builds from alu_op), followed by the is_jump ? pc+4 mux.
The forwarding path adds its own depth before the ALU: forward_unit compares
5-bit register numbers in EX, then the 3:1 forwarding mux, then the alu_src mux,
then the shifter/compare. The divider and multiplier arithmetic never appears
on a reported critical path. The limit is LUT depth in decode and select logic
that is recomputed every cycle in EX, even though all of it can be known a
cycle earlier in ID.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move every piece of EX-stage control decode into ID and register it in ID/EX,
so EX paths start at ready-made flop selects. The pipeline stays cycle-for-cycle
identical (same hazards, stalls, and forwarding sources), so IPC does not
change and the whole gain comes from Fmax.

1. One-hot ALU result select. ID maps alu_op (and is_jump) to a registered
   alu_sel_t with these fields:
   - result selects: r_add, r_sub, r_and, r_or, r_xor, r_slt, r_sltu, r_sll,
     r_sr, r_imm (LUI), r_mul_lo, r_mul_hi, r_div, r_rem, r_pc4 (JAL/JALR link)
   - operand-shaping flags: sra, mul_a_signed, mul_b_signed, div_signed
   EX computes the result as an AND-OR of `{32{sel}} & value` terms, with no
   alu_op decode on the path. The separate `is_jump ? pc+4 : alu_result` mux
   becomes one more one-hot term. Also:
   - Merge MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU into one 33x33 signed product. The top operand
     bits are `{signed_flag & x[31], x}`; take lo = prod[31:0] and
     hi = prod[63:32].
   - Merge SRL/SRA into one 33-bit arithmetic right shift of `{sra & a[31], a}`.
   - Keep the divider special cases (by-zero, INT_MIN/-1), keyed on the
     registered div_signed flag.
2. Early forwarding match. In ID, compare the incoming instruction's rs1/rs2
   against the current ID/EX.rd (qualified by ID/EX.ctrl.reg_write, rs!=0) and
   the current EX/MEM.rd (rs!=0). Register the four match bits into ID/EX.
   This is exact because:
   - When ID/EX loads a real instruction, EX/MEM and MEM/WB always advance too
     (stall_ex_mem = dmem_stall implies stall_id; load-use flushes ID/EX).
   - While a dmem stall freezes ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB keep their rd/ctrl
     (hold_wb clears only valid).
   - A load-use bubble re-decodes the same instruction in ID the next cycle.
   In EX, qualify each match with the post-trap producer reg_write, because
   misaligned JAL/JALR and misaligned loads clear reg_write after ID:
     s_ex  = m_ex  & EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write
     s_mem = m_mem & MEM/WB.ctrl.reg_write & !s_ex
   This keeps the baseline's priority and trap behaviour bit-exact.
3. Piped PC+4. IF already computes pc+4 for next_pc. Carry it through
   if_id_t and ID/EX (pc4 field) and use it for the r_pc4 link value and the
   pc_next fall-through/misalign value. This removes both pc+4 incrementers
   from EX. Without this step, the pc+4 carry chain feeding the result OR-tree
   becomes the new critical path on all three seeds.

Prototype evidence: I built the full change in a scratch copy and ran the exact
eval flow (yosys synth_gowin + 3 nextpnr seeds + Verilator CoreMark with
--bench --istall --dstall).
- Steps 1+2 only: 166.00 / 140.59 / 148.32 MHz, median 148.3 MHz (+16.8%).
  The pc+4 chain was then critical on every seed.
- Steps 1+2+3: 172.50 / 175.44 / 165.86 MHz, median 172.5 MHz (+35.8%).
  LUT4 9563 -> 7361, ALU 3704 -> 2112, FF 1866 -> 1914.
- CoreMark bracketed cycles: 4,491,485, identical to baseline.
- All five CRCs match and the UART output is byte-identical to baseline.
- selftest.elf full-trace cosim passes.
Formal was not run on the prototype.
With steps 1-3, the remaining critical path (about 5.7-6.0 ns) is the
AND-OR result tree itself.

title: Dual-source fetch: IF-local instruction replay store with registered lookahead
motivation:
CPI breakdown of the current bench core on the fitness workload (2K CoreMark,
-O3, ITERATIONS=10, --istall --dstall), taken from a full RVFI trace of
cores/bench/obj_dir/cosim_sim over the bracketed window: 2,922,017 retired
instructions in 4,491,485 cycles, so CPI = 1.537. That leaves 1.57M
cycles above CPI 1. A cycle model replaying the trace against the cosim's
xorshift ready sequence reproduces the measured count to within 0.03%
(4,492,620 vs 4,491,485). It splits those 1.57M cycles as:
  - imem backpressure:      ~820k  (io_imemReady=0 turns every fetch into a
                                   bubble; nothing overlaps it)
  - taken branch/JAL/JALR:  ~357k  (1-cycle EX redirect, 357.5k transfers)
  - load-use:               ~204k
  - dmem backpressure:      ~193k
No DIV/REM executes inside the timed window, and ALU/MUL work is single-cycle.
Instruction supply is the largest loss by far. It is also structural: the
front end has exactly one instruction source, the live imem bus. A
not-ready cycle is lost even when the PC is a hot-loop address fetched
thousands of times already. A plain fetch skid/queue cannot fix this
because fetch bandwidth is capped at 0.78 words/cycle. Modeling a 2-4 entry
decoupled fetch queue gives only +3.5% IPC. The sibling core cores/v1 measured
the same result (4.34M cycles, net regression after Fmax loss,
hyp-20260427-002-r1s1).
A second instruction source removes the cap for recently fetched code.
cores/v1 measured this as a replay table: cycles fell 18% on that core
(hyp-20260428-023-r10s1). Its registered-lookahead form kept full Fmax
(hyp-20260428-030-r12s2). My trace model for the bench core (no
predictors) gives these cycle reductions:
  direct-mapped  64 entries: +13.5%..15%    128 entries: +17.9%
  direct-mapped 256 entries: +20.6%         128 sets x 2 ways: +21.3%
  DM-256 without replay on the first cycle after a redirect: +18.2%
Fmax note (stated transparently): fpga/core_bench_si.sv and the formal
wrapper both tie io_imemReady=1'b1. If the design has the right shape,
yosys constant-folds the replay path out of the Fmax build. It then
reduces to the baseline netlist, which is what cores/v1 saw (+60 LUT4 for a
256-entry table). The eval's Fmax number is therefore blind to this
logic. To keep the claimed gain honest for a real stall-capable
build, the design must be timing-clean anyway: registered lookahead, and
no table read or tag compare on the live fetch->decode path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give the IF stage two instruction sources: the live imem bus, and a small
IF-local instruction replay store (L0 loop buffer). Fetch readiness
becomes fetch_ready = io_imemReady || replay_hit. When the bus stalls on a
PC whose word is held locally, the pipeline advances instead of bubbling.
Nothing else in the 5-stage pipeline changes.

Replay store (inside rtl/if_stage.sv or a new rtl/fetch_replay.sv):
  - 256 entries, direct-mapped, index = pc[9:2], tag = pc[31:10] (full
    upper PC, so no aliasing anywhere in the address space),
    data = 32-bit instruction word, plus a per-entry valid bit.
  - Only the valid-bit array is reset (clear all on reset). Tag and data
    arrays have NO reset, so they infer distributed RAM, not 1.7k flops.
  - Fill: on every cycle with io_imemReady=1, write {pc tag, io_imemData}
    at index(pc) and set its valid bit. This includes held, killed and
    wrong-path fetches: imem is a separate read-only port and FENCE.I is a
    NOP, so any accepted word is the true instruction at that PC.

Registered lookahead (the timing-clean part, proven in cores/v1):
  - Each cycle compute lookup_pc exactly as the PC register's next value:
      lookup_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : (!stall ? pc + 4 : pc)
    Read the table at index(lookup_pc) and tag-compare. Register
    cand_valid_q, cand_instr_q (and cand_pc_q).
  - Same-cycle fill bypass: if io_imemReady && lookup_pc == pc (a held
    PC), load io_imemData into the candidate directly, because the async
    read does not see this cycle's write. This makes an instruction fetched
    live during a load-use or dmem stall replayable on the next cycle.
  - Current-cycle use: replay_hit = cand_valid_q (optionally
    && cand_pc_q == pc; by construction the two always agree after
    reset). Instruction word into ID =
    io_imemReady ? io_imemData : cand_instr_q. Live data keeps priority.
    With io_imemReady tied to 1, the fetch->decode datapath is then
    bit-identical to today's.
  - Keep the existing NOP injection on flush/redirect, and keep redirect
    priority over stall for the PC register.

Hazard/control: stall_if = load_use || !fetch_ready || dmem_stall and
flush_if = redirect || !fetch_ready. The simplest wiring is to feed
fetch_ready into hazard_unit's imem_ready port from core.sv. No
combinational loop: fetch_ready depends only on io_imemReady and flops.
The lookahead read address depends on stall, but stall never depends on
the table read.

Bus-protocol note: on replay hits during io_imemReady=0 the PC (and
io_imemAddr) advances while ready is low. The ARCHITECTURE.md contract
and the cosim model treat ready as a per-cycle "serviced / not serviced"
flag with no request hold requirement, so this is legal.

Expected result: CoreMark cycles fall from ~4.49M to ~3.72M, a +20.6%
iter/cycle gain from the model. Median Fmax stays at the ~127 MHz
baseline (seed noise ±4%), so fitness rises by ~+18-21%. RVFI, the
decoder, trap discipline and the M-extension are untouched. Divider
removal is orthogonal and stacks on top of this.

Fallbacks if the implementer hits trouble:
  (a) If the redirect -> lookup_pc -> table path is ever a concern, drop
      redirect from lookup_pc and invalidate the candidate after a
      redirect. Modeled at +18.2% instead of +20.6%.
  (b) 128 entries direct-mapped is +17.9%. 128 sets x 2 ways with an MRU
      bit is +21.3% but adds fill-way logic; prefer DM-256.

title: Zero-bubble IF-stage predictor: predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT + 4-entry RAS, EX verify/repair
motivation:
The core has no prediction: every taken branch, JAL and JALR is resolved in
EX and redirects the PC, killing the instruction fetched that cycle. IF and ID
share a cycle (the IF/ID bundle is combinational), so each redirect costs
about 1 cycle.

Measured on the baseline cosim trace (CoreMark, --istall --dstall, bracketed
window, 10 iterations): 2,922,017 instructions and 4,491,485 cycles (CPI 1.537).
  - conditional branches: 529,588, of which 294,425 were taken (55.6%)
  - JAL: 49,367
  - JALR: 13,735, and every one is exactly `ret` (0x00008067)
  - average cycles to the next retirement: 2.44 after a taken branch, 1.38
    after a not-taken branch, 2.43 after a JAL, 1.31 after an ALU op. That
    gap confirms the ~1.06-cycle redirect penalty.
That adds up to 357,527 redirects, or about 8% of all bracketed cycles.

  - static BTFN: 111,175 mispredicts
  - bimodal 2-bit, 64 entries, index pc[7:2]^pc[13:8]: 41,566 mispredicts
  - bimodal 2-bit, 512 entries: 39,718 mispredicts
  - RAS hits: 13,723/13,735 at depth 4; 13,734 at depth 8

predecode the fetched instruction and steer the PC to pc+imm in that same
cycle, so a correctly predicted taken branch costs no cycles at all.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a next-PC predictor in the IF stage and a verify/repair step in EX.
Expected result: about 357.5k redirects drop to about 42k, saving about 316k
redirects x ~1.06 cycles, or about 335k cycles (4.49M -> ~4.16M). That is
roughly +8% iterations/cycle. The new logic sits alongside existing paths and
adds nothing to the current critical path (EX ALU -> EX/MEM, 7.87 ns), so
Fmax should stay about the same.

IF stage (all combinational from the PC register and imem_data):
  * Predecode the fetched word:
      is_br  = opcode 1100011 and funct3 not in {2,3}
      is_jal = opcode 1101111
      is_ret = instr == 32'h00008067
    Extract immB and immJ.
  * BHT: 64 x 2-bit saturating counters in flops, reset to 2'b10 (weakly
    taken). Index = pc[7:2] ^ pc[13:8].
  * pred_taken =
        (is_jal && !immJ[1])
      | (is_br && bht[idx][1] && !immB[1])
      | is_ret
    The immX[1] guard means IF never steers to a misaligned target, so the
    existing misalign-trap path in EX is unchanged.
  * pred_target = is_ret ? ras[top] : pc + (is_jal ? immJ : immB)
  * PC priority: reset > redirect(EX) > stall_if (hold) > pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4
  * RAS: 4-entry circular stack with no count or valid bit. A `ret` popped
    from an empty or corrupt stack just gets a wrong target, which EX catches
    as an ordinary mispredict.
      - push pc+4 on an accepted JAL/JALR with rd==x1
      - pop on an accepted `ret`
  * "Accepted" means: imem ready and !stall_if and !redirect. That is exactly
    the condition under which the IF instruction is latched into ID/EX while
    the PC takes next_pc.
  * Accepted instructions are never flushed later: the only flush of the IF
    instruction happens in the same cycle as an EX redirect, and that cycle
    is excluded from "accepted". So RAS updates are architectural and need no
    checkpoint or repair.
  * Carry pred_taken (1 bit) and pred_target (32 bits) in if_id_t and
    id_ex_t. Force pred_taken=0 whenever the IF bundle is a NOP
    (flush/redirect/imem stall).

EX verify/repair:
  * Let taken_eff = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault. This is
    today's `redirect`.
  * Let ret_mismatch = is_jalr && ({jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0} != pred_target).
  * redirect = pred_taken ? (!taken_eff || ret_mismatch) : taken_eff
  * redirect_target = (pred_taken && !taken_eff) ? pc+4
                      : (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
  * For predicted JAL/branches the IF target equals EX's pc+imm by
    construction. The catch-all `pred_taken && !taken_eff -> pc+4` also
    covers a prediction on an encoding the full decoder rejects.
  * pc_next and every RVFI field stay computed from actual semantics, exactly
    as today, so the contract is untouched.

BHT update in EX:
  * Update when id_ex.valid && is_branch && !stall_ex_mem, so a dmem stall
    that holds the branch in EX updates it only once.
  * Use a second read port indexed by EX pc to read-modify-write the counter
    (the table is only 128 flops).
  * Write direction = the raw branch_taken.

The replay store already hides most imem stalls, and the eval's Fmax build
ties io_imemReady=1. Every taken branch, JAL and JALR resolves in EX and
kills the word IF fetched that cycle. IF/ID is combinational, so each
redirect costs 1 cycle.

Measured on the bracketed CoreMark window (2,922,015 retired instructions,
RVFI trace from cores/bench/obj_dir/cosim_sim --istall --dstall):
  - 357,527 taken transfers: 294.4k taken branches, 49.4k JAL, 13.7k JALR
    (all `ret`)
  - that is ~9.6% of the current 3,724,565-cycle window
The last predictor (hyp-20260925-003-r1s2) removed ~316k of these cycles
but lost ~18% Fmax. It predecoded io_imemData, which fpga/core_bench_si.sv
drives from an LFSR flop, then ran an immB/immJ pc+imm adder and the RAS
into next_pc in the same cycle. That put a decode + 32-bit carry-chain +
PC-mux path inside the combined IF/ID cycle.

I ran synth + nextpnr seed 1 on the current bench RTL. It reproduces
179.28 MHz. The critical path (5.58 ns) is NOT in the front end. It is the
EX-stage `in.pc + in.imm` / `pc + 4` carry chains running from the ID/EX
flops into the PC-D / EX/MEM pc_next cone. The IF PC register itself has
slack. So a predictor is viable if it (a) reads only the PC register,
never the instruction word, (b) needs no adder in IF, and (c) moves those
EX adders into ID so the verify step is flop-based.

allocate-on-taken, EX update visible 1 instruction later, JALR never
predicted:

    16 / 8               81,245        276,282
    32 / 6               83,633        273,894
    32 / 8               67,904        289,623   <- proposed
    64 / 6               63,272        294,255
   128 / 6               57,756        299,771
With 4-bit tags, non-branch instructions alias onto hot entries
(32/4 = only 222k saved), so the tag must be about 8 bits. A 14-bit stored
target (pc[15:2]) loses nothing because CoreMark text is < 64 KB.

redirects.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small PC-indexed branch target buffer to IF. In the same cycle it
steers next_pc from the PC register alone: no predecode, no adder. EX
checks the prediction with flop-sourced comparisons. Correctly predicted
taken branches and JALs then cost 0 cycles instead of 1.

IF (if_stage.sv):
  * BTB: 32 entries, direct-mapped, index = pc[6:2], tag = pc[14:7]
    (8 bits), target = pc[15:2] of the destination (14 bits), 2-bit
    counter.
  * Keep a reset-cleared vector pt[31:0] = "valid && ctr[1]" in flops.
    Tag, target and ctr go in resetless arrays (LUTRAM if yosys maps it,
    flops otherwise; both are fine).
  * pred_taken  = pt[pc[6:2]] && (tag[pc[6:2]] == pc[14:7])
    pred_target = {pc[31:16], tgt[pc[6:2]], 2'b00}
  * next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target
            : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc_plus4
    Priority is unchanged: reset > redirect > !stall.
  * Nothing in this loop reads imem_data. Its depth is PC flop -> 32:1
    read -> 8-bit eq -> 30-bit 2:1 select (merged with the redirect mux)
    -> PC D, about 5 LUT levels with no carry chain.
  * Send pred_taken to ID with the IF bundle, forced to 0 whenever the
    bundle is a NOP (flush / redirect / fetch miss). Also send pc_plus4
    and the BTB read metadata btb_hit (valid && tag_eq) and btb_ctr[1:0],
    so EX can update the counter without a second read port.
  * Replay-store correctness: the lookahead read address must become the
    true next PC:
      rd_idx/rd_tag from (redirect ? redirect_target
                          : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc_plus4)
    The same-cycle fill bypass must fire whenever that next PC equals
    pc, not only on redirect (e.g. a predicted `j .`). In the Fmax build
    (imemReady=1) all of this still folds away.

ID (id_stage.sv):
  * Register pred_taken, btb_hit, btb_ctr and pc_plus4 into ID/EX.
  * Compute br_tgt = in.pc + imm here and register it. This is the
    branch/JAL target. The adder runs from the fetched word after
    imm_gen and ends at a flop, so it has no downstream logic.

EX (ex_stage.sv):
  * Use in.br_tgt in place of `in.pc + in.imm`, for both branch_target
    and the JAL arm of jump_target. Use in.pc_plus4 in place of
    `in.pc + 32'd4`, for both the link value and pc_next. This removes
    today's critical carry chain from EX.
  * New input pc_if: the IF PC register (io_imemAddr). While ID/EX holds
    a valid instruction, pc_if is always the address IF fetched as that
    instruction's successor, because the PC register and ID/EX advance
    together and every other case either holds both or bubbles ID/EX.
  * taken_eff = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
    (this is today's redirect)
  * redirect =

    semantics. The retired stream is unchanged; only fetch timing
    changes.

    waiting in EX can raise redirect (to pc+4). Change flush_id to
    (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall && !div_stall so the held DIV
    is never wiped. PC/IF behaviour stays the same: redirect overrides
    the stall and IF emits a NOP. When the DIV finishes, the still-
    asserted redirect bubbles ID/EX exactly once.

to the true pc_next, so riscv-formal (unconstrained imem) and cosim

pt vector.

title: Stall-decoupled memory pipeline: posted store buffer + MEM-local data replay store, 1024-entry IF replay store
motivation:
Measured, not estimated. I rebuilt the current RTL's cosim, captured the
CoreMark RVFI trace, and wrote a trace-driven cycle model that replays the
harness's exact xorshift ready sequence (imem draw then dmem draw per
cycle). It reproduces the logged window exactly (3,724,565 cycles, start
marker at cycle 13,086). Window: 2.92M insns, CPI 1.275. Bubble cycles
over the whole run:
  - EX redirect (1 bubble per taken branch/JAL/JALR):  ~360K
  - load-use (66% load->branch, 29% load->load address): ~204K
  - dmem backpressure (EX/MEM mem op while io_dmemReady=0
    freezes the whole pipeline; 684K mem ops):          ~193K
  - fetch miss (256-entry IF replay store misses):       ~52K
Redirect and load-use sit on the EX/IF paths that decide Fmax. Every past
attempt there lost more Fmax than it saved in cycles (r1s2, r4s0, r4s2).
The two bus-stall buckets (~245K cycles, 6.6% of runtime) are different:
formal/wrapper_si.sv and fpga/core_bench_si.sv both tie io_imemReady=1 and
io_dmemReady=1, so logic that is consulted only when a bus stalls
constant-folds out of the FPGA netlist. I confirmed this on this core: with
RP_IDX_BITS raised 8->10, yosys gives the same 7619 cells and connectivity
(only src attributes differ), nextpnr seed 1 gives exactly 179.28 MHz (same
as the parent), and the real cosim gives 3,683,593 cycles, matching the
model to the cycle.
Caveat: the LUT-RAM area these structures would cost in a real SoC is
invisible to this eval because both benches tie the ready signals to 1. The
accepted r1s1 IF replay store already relies on the same property.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the MEM stage tolerate dmem backpressure the way if_stage already
tolerates imem backpressure, and widen the IF replay store. The pipeline
then freezes only on a true miss. Modeled result for exactly the fold-safe
rules below: 3,724,565 -> 3,501,791 cycles (+6.36% iter/cycle). Remaining
dmem-stall cycles drop from 193K to 9.6K and fetch misses from 52K to 9K.
Fmax should be unchanged because the FPGA netlist should be identical.
(Idealized upper bound: +6.5%. Merging byte/halfword stores into the data
store would add only 0.1% and is not fold-safe, so skip it.)

1. IF replay store 256 -> 1024 entries (if_stage.sv RP_IDX_BITS 8 -> 10).
   Alone, this was measured at +1.11% in the real cosim with an identical
   P&R result.

2. Posted store buffer (1 entry) in mem_stage: sb_valid, sb_addr,
   sb_wdata (lane-replicated), sb_wen.
     drain    = sb_valid && dmem_ready   (the buffer owns the bus that cycle)
     bus_free = dmem_ready && !sb_valid  (MEM op may use the bus)
     push     = aligned STORE in EX/MEM && !dmem_ready && !sb_valid
     sb_valid_next = push || (sb_valid && !dmem_ready)
   Push ONLY when !dmem_ready. With ready tied to 1, sb_valid_next is then
   the constant 0 (its reset value) and the whole buffer folds. Do NOT let
   a store push while the buffer is draining: that makes the next state
   depend on itself (Q & X), and yosys will not fold that.
   Bus ports: io_dmemAddr/WData/WEn come from the buffer when sb_valid,
   otherwise from EX/MEM as today. io_dmemREn = !sb_valid && aligned load.
   These ports must depend on REGISTERS ONLY, never combinationally on
   io_dmemReady. main.cpp samples io_dmemRData from io_dmemAddr BEFORE
   eval(), and applies writes when WEn && ready after eval().

3. MEM-local data replay store, 256 entries, direct-mapped. Index
   addr[9:2], tag addr[31:10]. Only the valid bits reset; the data array
   is {tag, word} with no reset. Lookup is combinational off the
   registered EX/MEM.alu_result. It is stall-only, so it folds.
   Writes must never depend on reading the array (no read-modify-write),
   otherwise the read port feeds the array's own write and it will not fold:
     - load served by the bus (bus_free) to RAM (addr < 0x0010_0000):
       write {tag, io_dmemRData}, set valid
     - SW that completes (direct or pushed) to RAM: write {tag, wdata}, set valid
     - SB/SH that completes: clear valid[idx] unconditionally (no tag check)
   The array stays coherent with memory at all times, including while a
   store waits in the buffer, because it is updated when the store
   completes in MEM, not when the buffer drains.

4. Completion / stall rule (replaces hazard_unit's
   dmem_stall = !dmem_ready && ex_mem_mem_op):
     load  completes iff bus_free || l0_hit
     store completes iff !sb_valid   (direct if ready, else push)
     misaligned (trapping) mem ops never need the bus -> never stall
     EBREAK in EX/MEM with sb_valid -> stall, so the last UART bytes are
       on the bus before the cosim stops at EBREAK retirement
     mem_stall = (valid aligned mem op && !completes) || ebreak guard
   Load data source: rdata_eff = bus_free ? io_dmemRData : l0_word. This
   feeds the existing shift/extend logic and MEM/WB.mem_rdata, so RVFI
   mem_rdata is the true memory word. hold_mem_wb / stall_ex_mem keep their
   current meaning, now driven by mem_stall.

title: Prune redundant redirect/load-use terms from IF/ID NOP mux and ID/EX flush/stall fan-out
motivation:
r4s2's timing analysis found that on this ~179 MHz core the worst paths
are pre-existing control nets, including imem(LFSR) -> load-use ->
a 1.75 ns flush_id fan-out into the ID/EX synchronous reset. In the
current RTL, three control terms are logically redundant but yosys
can't prove that, so they stay on timed paths:
  (1) if_stage NOP-injects the IF/ID bundle on `redirect` (flush_if =
      redirect || fetch_miss). When redirect=1, flush_id kills ID/EX anyway
      (or ID/EX holds on dmem_stall), so the NOP mux only puts EX's
      branch comparator -> redirect in front of the regfile read address,
      decoder, imm_gen and load-use compare, all feeding ID/EX D inputs.
  (2) stall_id includes load_use_hazard, but whenever load_use=1 and
      !dmem_stall, flush_id=1 takes priority, and with dmem_stall=1
      stall_id is already 1. So the imem -> rs compare -> load_use path
      drives the ID/EX clock-enable (~200 flops) for no reason.
  (3) flush_id synchronously clears every ID/EX bit (~200 flops: pc,
      rs1/rs2 values, imm, instr, ...), but a bubble only needs its
      side-effect bits cleared: valid, reg_write, mem_read, mem_write,
      is_branch, is_jump, is_div. Every datapath field of a bubble is
      don't-care downstream (forward_unit gates on reg_write, hazard_unit
      on mem_read, EX redirect on is_branch/is_jump, MEM on mem_read/
      mem_write, WB/RVFI on valid).

title: Resetless LUT-RAM register file: move the 32x32 regfile out of 1024 flops + two 32:1 mux trees into RAM16SDP4
motivation:
Measured on this machine with the eval's own flow (synth.tcl +
core_bench_si.sv + nextpnr_run.sh). A fresh build of the current RTL
reproduces the log exactly: 7575 cells, seeds 1/2/3 = 171.00 / 174.73 /
167.95 MHz (seeds 4/5 = 158.91 / 180.86). Its critical path is EX
(ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op -> ALU result mux -> EX/MEM). 2.24 ns of its 5.85 ns
is routing, including a 1.18 ns hop across 11 tiles, so the core is
limited by how spread out it is, not by its logic depth. This is the same
effect the r3s1 divider eviction exploited.

The single biggest block in the fabric is the register file. reg_file.sv
has a synchronous reset that clears all 32 registers. That reset stops
yosys from inferring RAM, so the array becomes 1024 DFFE plus two 32:1
read-mux trees. It is about half the FFs and more than half the LUTs:
LUT1-4 = 4669, DFFE = 1146. Nothing in the contract needs the reset.
riscv-formal's reg check only compares reads against writes it has
observed (k-induction already starts from an arbitrary regfile). The
cosim ISS and CoreMark only need the registers to be 0 at power-up, and
an initial block gives that (RAM16SDP4 INIT / Verilator time 0).

Prototype (exact RTL below, all other files byte-identical):
  cells 7575 -> 3738; LUT1..4 4669 -> 1954; DFFE 1146 -> 131;
  MUX2_LUT5 373 -> 231; +32 RAM16SDP4 (of 648); DSP/BSRAM unchanged.
  nextpnr seeds 1/2/3 = 206.06 / 222.82 / 210.57 MHz (median 210.6).
  An earlier identical-logic build gave 205.68 / 209.73 / 219.35 /
  198.14 / 211.69. Its worst seed (198) beats the parent's best (181),
  so the two distributions do not overlap.
  Verilator CoreMark (--bench --istall --dstall): all five CRCs match,
  "Correct operation validated.", window = 3,501,791 cycles, identical
  to the parent's logged count.
Projected fitness: 10 / 3,501,791 x 210.6 MHz = 601 iter/s vs 488.32
(+23%).

Variants I measured and rejected (do NOT add them):
  - Valid-bit squash (no ID/EX reset or NOP-inject on redirect/load-use;
    side effects gated by valid in EX): alone 165.6/162.4/159.1 MHz;
    with the LUT-RAM regfile 204.3/181.0/187.4. It stacks badly because
    the valid gating adds LUT levels to the EX result/ctrl paths.
  - Moving the write-first bypass out of ID (register a per-operand
    "WB hit" + WB data in ID/EX and mux in EX): 192.0/152.7/190.7/
    169.6/160.2 MHz. The extra EX mux lands on the EX critical path.
    With the LUT-RAM regfile the reported worst path on some seeds is
    MEM/WB.rd -> bypass compare -> ID/EX.rs_val (4.86 ns). It is still
    cheaper in ID than in EX, so keep the bypass exactly where it is.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Build a lookahead "offset predictor". It never stores targets, never
compares targets, and never touches imem_data on the PC path.

Key idea. The table entry for a taken BRANCH/JAL at address B lives
under key B-4, so the PC register X looks up whether the instruction
at X+4 is a taken branch. Registering that one cycle early takes the
table read and tag compare off the PC-D path. The entry stores the
branch's immediate (offset), not its target. When the prediction
fires, the next fetch is pc + offset, computed by the existing
sequential PC adder with a flop operand in place of the constant 4. So
the predicted target is always pc + imm of whatever word sits at pc.
Correctness needs only a cheap bit-compare of the fetched word's
immediate against the stored offset, not a 30-bit target compare.

IF (if_stage.sv)
  * Table: 32 entries, index pc[6:2], tag pc[19:7] (13 bits, the whole
    legal 1 MB space above the index), off = imm[12:2] (11 bits; bit 1
    is always 0 because misaligned targets are never trained), ctr[1:0].
    Tag/off/ctr go in a resetless array (LUTRAM). A 32-bit valid vector
    is reset-cleared flops.
    hit  = valid[pc[6:2]] && tag[pc[6:2]] == pc[19:7]
    take = hit && ctr[1]
    Because the tag covers pc[19:7], any legal PC that hits is exactly
    the PC that trained the entry. A speculative fetch can therefore
    only go to a target the program already executed, so the cosim's
    imem OOB check (io_imemAddr outside [0, 1 MB) is sticky failure)
    can never trip on a wrong-path prediction. Do NOT shrink the tag.
  * Registered prediction for the instruction at the CURRENT pc, same
    enable as the PC register (hold on stall, redirect overrides):
      redirect           : pred_q <= 0, lk_q <= 0
      stall              : hold everything
      pred_q (taken now) : pred_q <= 0, lk_q <= 0  (no lookup for a
                           predicted target; costs only ~1K)
      else               : lk_q <= 1, pred_q <= take,
                           off_q <= off, hit_q <= hit, ctr_q <= ctr
    off_q/hit_q/ctr_q/ctr may capture freely under the same enable.
    Only pred_q and lk_q need redirect in D.
  * Sequential next PC:
      pc_seq[31:2] = pc[31:2] + (pred_q ? sext(off_q) : 30'd1)
      next_pc      = redirect ? redirect_target : {pc_seq, 2'b00}
    This is today's pc+4 carry chain with a flop-driven operand. The
    PC-D path's timing is set by the late redirect select, and the
    operand LUT sits in the early leg, so this adds no depth there.
    Priority is unchanged: reset > redirect > !stall.
  * Replay store: the lookahead read address becomes
    redirect ? redirect_target : pc_seq. Never allocate an entry with
    off == 0, which excludes `j .` and `beq x,x,.`. Then pc_seq != pc
    whenever the PC advances without a redirect, and the existing
    same-cycle bypass condition stays correct. All of this still folds
    under io_imemReady = 1.
  * IF bundle to ID: pred = pred_q && fetch_ready (0 on a fetch-miss
    NOP; redirect bubbles are already cleared by flush_id). Also send
    off_q, and bp_hit = lk_q && hit_q, bp_ctr = ctr_q for the update.
    Do NOT add redirect in front of the combinational IF/ID
    instruction (r4s2 lesson).

ID (id_stage.sv)
  * pred_ok = pred && word is BRANCH or JAL && imm matches sext(off_q).
    Use a raw-bit compare with no imm_gen and no adder:
      opcode: instr[6:4]==3'b110 && instr[1:0]==2'b11
              && instr[3]==instr[2]      (BRANCH=00 / JAL=11; JALR out)
      common: instr[31]==off[12], instr[30:25]==off[10:5]
      BRANCH (instr[3]=0): instr[7]==off[11], instr[11:9]==off[4:2],
                           instr[8]==0 (imm[1])
      JAL    (instr[3]=1): instr[20]==off[11], instr[24:22]==off[4:2],
                           instr[21]==0, instr[19:12]=={8{off[12]}}
    That is about 4 LUT levels from the fetched word, ending at a single
    ID/EX flop, with nothing downstream in the same cycle.
  * ID/EX gains 4 bits: pred, pred_ok, bp_hit, bp_ctr[1:0] (5 flops).
    Reset/flush '0 clears them.

EX (ex_stage.sv)
  * taken_eff = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
    (today's redirect).
    redirect = taken_eff ? !in.pred_ok : (in.pred && !div_wait)
    Every input except taken_eff is a flop, so this is one LUT on the
    existing late signal. Gating the not-taken arm with !div_wait means
    a (formal-only) prediction on a DIV redirects once, when the DIV
    leaves EX. hazard_unit and flush_id stay untouched.
  * redirect_target = taken_eff ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                : in.pc + 4
    A predicted-taken branch that falls through returns to pc+4.
    Write the per-bit select so the late branch_cond picks between two
    early, flop/adder-derived candidates.
  * EX/MEM gains bp_hit and bp_ctr (3 flops). pc_next, the misalign
    trap and every RVFI field are unchanged. The retired stream is
    identical; only fetch timing changes.

MEM (mem_stage.sv) trains the table from registered EX/MEM state, off
every EX path:
    upd = valid && (is_branch || (is_jump && !is_jalr)) && !is_illegal
          && (taken || bp_hit)
    taken = branch_taken || is_jump
    off   = imm[12:2], decoded by bit-select from EX/MEM.instr
            (B vs J chosen by instr[3]). Allocate only if the offset
            fits 13 bits, imm[1]==0 and off != 0.
    key   = EX/MEM.pc - 4  (idx [6:2], tag [19:7]; a short decrement
            on a flop)
    ctr'  = bp_hit ? sat(ctr +/- 1) : (JAL ? 2'b11 : 2'b10)
    Not taken with no hit: no write. A write repeated while EX/MEM is
    held by mem_stall is idempotent. Export upd/idx/tag/off/ctr' to
    if_stage's write port.

Expected: cycles 3.50M -> ~3.22M (+8.9% iter/cycle). Added state is
about 60 flops, ~14 RAM16SDP4 and 4+3 pipeline bits. There is no new
compare or adder on redirect or PC-D. Fitness holds up if Fmax stays
above ~157 MHz (break-even).

Acceptance: cosim --istall --dstall must keep the CoreMark CRCs and give
about 3.22M cycles (if it is above 3.30M, the predictor is not firing).
Run synth_gowin, then check `stat` against the parent: MULT36X36/DPX9B
counts must be unchanged, and there should be no more than ~16 new
RAM16SDP4 and about +60 DFF. Report nextpnr on 3 seeds.

lesson: - 2026-09-25 hyp-20260925-003-r6s2 (regression, +1.10%): A lookahead offset predictor (a 32-entry table keyed by pc-4 that stores only imm[12:2] plus a 2-bit counter in 14 RAM16SDP4, a registered pred_q that swaps the constant 4 in the existing PC adder for sext(off_q), a raw-bit imm-vs-offset check into one ID/EX flop, and redirect = taken_eff ? !pred_ok : pred with no target compare) is the first predictor here that didn't lose fitness: the prototype's cosim hit the modeled cycles (3.50M->3.22M, -8.1%) and the Fmax cost fell to ~7% (171->~159 MHz implied, vs -17% for r4s2's target-storing BTB and worse for r1s2's imem_data predecode), so storing offsets instead of targets, reusing the PC adder, checking with bit-compares and registering the lookup a cycle early is the right shape; but +1.1% on the r5s1 parent lost to the round's +23% LUT-RAM regfile, so re-apply it on the r6s1 core, where it must keep ≥~194 of ~211 MHz to pay, and start from the prototype's single taken_eff mux in EX (seeds 169/176/181 MHz) rather than the submitted branch_cond-split redirect, since it isn't clear whether the ~159 MHz came from that split or from seed noise.
